extracted.intended_audience: academics and public-health professionals (and other subject-matter experts) who want to pitch op-eds to news outlets
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and sending a short, effective email pitch and attached op-ed to digital or print news outlets (including subject line, pitch body, author credibility, fit, formatting, and follow-up).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity and conciseness
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitches should be as short as possible—two very short paragraphs and less than 200 words is a good rule of thumb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the pitch to two very short paragraphs and under ~200 words. Editors are very busy; long pitches reduce the chance they will be read. Structure tightly: a one-sentence argument plus a short contextualizing sentence is typical. Avoid long-winded background or extended literature reviews in the pitch.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-paragraph summary answering core questions
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first paragraph, briefly summarize your idea/message, being sure to include answers to the following questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opening paragraph should succinctly state the piece's central idea and explicitly address: why this message/idea is important; why it is important right now; and what you are adding to the conversation. This is the paragraph that must convince an editor the piece matters and fits their readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: State why the message/idea is important
rubrics_metrics.description: Why is this message/idea important? In the most compelling terms possible, state your argument, shooting for a single sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft a single, compelling sentence that states your main argument and give only the necessary context for an editor to understand the target audience and stakes. Anti-pattern: assuming everyone knows the larger context and jumping straight into argument without clarifying why it matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish timeliness (Why it matters now)
rubrics_metrics.description: Why is it important right now? Make a case that what you have to say is timely—the more urgent the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a clear news hook or reason for urgency (link to current events, anniversaries, holidays, cultural happenings, new data, policy windows). Be creative and explicit about the connection to current events to justify immediate placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain your unique contribution (What you add)
rubrics_metrics.description: What are you adding to the conversation? Do you have a counterintuitive or otherwise fresh perspective? New research findings?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate novelty or distinctive perspective—explain succinctly how your piece adds value beyond what's already been said. If the topic has been recently covered in the outlet, note how your angle differs; otherwise consider pitching elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the case for the author (qualifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Your pitch should also make clear why you are qualified to write about this topic. Do this in a single, short sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include only credentials that directly support your authority to weigh in. If you have previous op-eds or letters published, state that and link to examples (e.g., 'My ideas have appeared in outlet-x, outlet-y'). Avoid long CVs—one concise sentence suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do your homework: fit with the publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure your op-ed is a good fit for the publication you are pitching. Get to know what they cover and the tone of the pieces they publish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the outlet’s op-ed section to understand topical priorities and tone; if the outlet has recently covered your topic, consider another venue. Tailor pitch language and framing to the publication’s style and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the outlet's submission guidelines and formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Always copy and paste the piece into the body of your email beneath your pitch. Check formatting to be sure you haven’t lost paragraph breaks, hyperlinks, or other formatting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put the full piece in the email body (not as an attachment) and confirm paragraph breaks, hyperlinks, and any required formatting are preserved. Consider ending the pitch with a line like: 'The piece is copied below. Do you see a fit for [name of outlet]?' to prompt a response.

rubrics_metrics.name: No email attachments
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not send the op-ed as an email attachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors prefer the text in the body of the message to avoid downloads and compatibility issues. Attaching files can reduce the likelihood of your piece being read; paste the piece into the email instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject line: be clear and attention-grabbing
rubrics_metrics.description: Make clear that this is a pitch. Think how best to grab a busy editor’s attention as they scan their jammed email box.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a concise subject that signals 'Pitch' and summarizes the angle. Consider highlighting institutional affiliation (e.g., Harvard) or a personal referral/connection if you have one. Example formats: 'Pitch: [short hook] (via Your Name)' or 'Pitch: [Topic] (by [Institution])'. Tailor to the outlet and avoid vague subject lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up strategy and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: After you pitch — be sure to follow up. If the topic is blazing hot and timely, follow up in 24 hours; otherwise wait 3–5 days. If no response, send additional polite follow-ups spaced 24–48 hours apart with clear subject-line signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested sequence: 1) If urgent, follow up in ~24 hours with a forwarded original and short note (e.g., 'Chance to look?'). 2) If no response, 24–48 hours after first follow-up send a note with subject like 'Assume no?' and a brief message indicating you may place elsewhere. 3) If still no response, 24–48 hours later send a final note with subject 'Moving on' or 'Pitching elsewhere' and thank them. Adjust timing based on news cycle. Always be polite and respectful—editors are busy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politeness and professionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Be polite and respectful in all communications with editors, recognizing they are dealing with many stories on any given day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep follow-ups short and courteous; do not pester. Use professional language and gratitude even when indicating you will pitch elsewhere. Tone can influence future opportunities—maintain professional relationships.
